summary: A developer can start building the sample now: all required data‑plane tools (documentdb MCP), language runtimes (Python, Node), and the DocumentDB domain skills are present and authoritative Microsoft Learn pages exist for every cold-answer item. Several cold answers were either outdated or described a neighbouring product (Cosmos DB account / older Cosmos Mongo API) and must be corrected before code is written. Missing local utilities and optional accelerators (notably mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) are not blocking but would speed verification and infra work.
summary_points: The data-plane MCP server 'documentdb' and the relevant DocumentDB skills are available — the build can start against the live cluster.

Multiple cold answers confuse Cosmos DB account (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) or older Cosmos Mongo API connection strings with the current Azure DocumentDB vCore product; the builder must use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the mongoClusters CLI/group.

Connection strings use mongodb+srv and a .global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com host form and require tls/oidc/specific authMechanism options — do not reuse older :10255 / .mongo.cosmos.azure.com examples.

Vector and full-text APIs are DocumentDB-native (cosmosSearch / createSearchIndexes) — the sample should use the documentdb-vector-search and documentdb-full-text-search skills for index creation and queries rather than Atlas/third-party syntax.
No blocker: missing CLI tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform) would help but are optional; install mongosh if manual interactive checks are desired.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource is used for MongoDB-compatible clusters).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) clusters are deployed as resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB). The vCore-managed MongoDB offering uses the mongoClusters resource, not databaseAccounts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical overlap: Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) are the classic Cosmos service resources and older docs / examples often show Mongo API under databaseAccounts, causing an agent to conflate the two.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (older Cosmos DB account docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in deployment code or CLI will create the wrong resource (Cosmos account) and not the vCore mongoClusters; Bicep/Terraform templates will be invalid for the target service.
improvements: Update quickstarts and sample READMEs that previously referenced 'databaseAccounts' for Mongo workloads to explicitly call out Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and link to the mongoClusters docs.

Add a one-line deprecation note on any Learn page that still shows 'create az cosmosdb ... --kind MongoDB' for vCore clusters, pointing readers to the mongoClusters command or the az cosmosdb mongocluster subcommands.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name my-docdb-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session. (az cosmosdb is part of the core Azure CLI, not an extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The current authoritative CLI surface for vCore clusters is the 'mongocluster' subcommands (az cosmosdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster create) or direct az resource create calls targeting resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters'. There are dedicated 'mongocluster' command groups (preview) rather than the older generic az cosmosdb create for databaseAccounts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB CLI patterns used az cosmosdb create for accounts; the vCore mongoClusters surface either exposes 'mongocluster' subgroups (preview) or requires creating the mongoClusters resource type directly.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (older docs/examples still present)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with --kind MongoDB will create a databaseAccount resource (RU model) not the vCore mongoClusters the sample expects; this leads to wrong capacity model and incompatible connection strings.
improvements: Add a clear sentence on the 'Quickstart' landing pages: 'To create a vCore Azure DocumentDB cluster use az cosmosdb mongocluster create or az resource create --resource-type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters"; do not use az cosmosdb create for vCore clusters.'
The Azure CLI docs should highlight the distinct command subgroup and link to mongoClusters examples.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (set kind: 'MongoDB'...). Terraform: resource 'azurerm_cosmosdb_account' (set capabilities for MongoDB).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the Bicep / ARM / Terraform resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (API versions shown on the mongoClusters resource page). Terraform's azurerm provider exposes azurerm_mongo_cluster or AzAPI modules / azapi targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for the vCore offering; do not use azurerm_cosmosdb_account for vCore mongoClusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy Cosmos DB samples and many community snippets show Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the Cosmos (RU) API; the vCore product uses a dedicated resource type.

confusion_sources.title: azurerm_cosmosdb_account docs and older Terraform examples

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account, they would deploy a RU-based Cosmos account or fail to deploy the intended vCore cluster; infra-as-code would not match the live cluster expectations.
improvements: Make the Bicep & Terraform quickstarts for DocumentDB explicit: show the 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' resource type and an example azurerm_mongo_cluster or azapi-based snippet in the repo README.
Deprecate older templates that show databaseAccounts for Mongo workloads, or add a prominent banner explaining when to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters use an SRV-style connection string example: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (the driver must be given TLS/tls=true, retryWrites=false, and the correct authMechanism or OIDC settings when using Entra auth). Do not rely on the older :10255 / .mongo.cosmos.azure.com examples.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API and some Cosmos DB Quickstarts used a non-SRV endpoint with port 10255 (or 10260 local gateway), leading agents to present that as canonical. The vCore mongoClusters use SRV hostnames and different host suffixes.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo connection examples (community posts / older MS docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host/port or leaving retryWrites at the driver default may cause connection errors or subtle behavior differences (retryable writes not supported).
improvements: Quickstart pages should show an explicit single canonical example for vCore clusters (SRV-style) and label older :10255 examples as 'Cosmos DB (RU) legacy style' to avoid conflation.
Add a short checklist in the sample README: 'Use mongodb+srv and ensure retryWrites=false and tls=true; use OIDC authMechanism for Entra ID.'

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Some MongoDB-compatible offerings use RU/s; vCore-style clusters expose M-family tiers billed by vCores. If you instead deploy a Cosmos DB account for Mongo API you will see RU/s billing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is provisioned and billed on compute tiers (M10, M20, M30, etc.), i.e., a vCore/compute-tier based model plus storage. The RU/s (Request Units) model applies to Cosmos DB RU-based accounts, not to vCore DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing model: vCores and storage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both RU-based Cosmos DB and vCore-based DocumentDB live under Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace historically; community docs and some automation still show RU-based flows, causing ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB RU/s based examples (older / different SKU docs)

confusions.build_risk: Selecting the wrong provisioning model in examples or docs would cause the sample to target an account whose billing/throughput semantics differ from the live cluster; benchmarks and capacity decisions would be invalid.
improvements: Add a short explicit paragraph to the sample README: 'This sample targets a vCore M30 DocumentDB cluster (compute tier). If you provision a Cosmos DB RU account instead, connection strings and billing semantics differ.'
Annotate Azure CLI/Bicep quickstarts to explicitly set computeTier for mongoClusters and avoid references to RU/s for vCore examples.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported DB authentication for Mongo clients is username/password (SCRAM-SHA-256 / SCRAM-SHA-1). Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) based authentication for MongoDB drivers is not generally supported as an alternative to SCRAM; Azure AD is used for control-plane operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native SCRAM (username/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane authentication. The service exposes OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism options (example connection string uses authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and mongodb+srv). Managed identities / client ID flows are documented for connecting via Compass, mongosh, or drivers when the cluster has Entra auth enabled.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected older limitations or other services where AD/OIDC isn't exposed to the Mongo data-plane; in DocumentDB vCore Entra ID / OIDC is explicitly supported for data-plane auth.

confusion_sources.title: Legacy statements and community posts saying AD is only for management plane

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is not available, they may hardcode username/password in the environment or choose the wrong auth flow; conversely, if they assume Entra ID always works but the cluster hasn't enabled it, the connection will fail. The sample must document both supported modes and how to enable/register identities.
improvements: Add an explicit small how‑to paragraph on the sample README showing two connection examples: SCRAM URI and an OIDC example with the required authMechanism and OIDC properties, with links to the Learn page.
Ensure the az/portal quickstarts for mongoClusters highlight the '--auth-allowed-modes' option and link to the Entra ID connection docs.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for data-plane operations (e.g. pymongo for Python). There is no separate data-plane, Mongo-API-specific Azure SDK; for management tasks use the Azure CLI/SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane operations. Management and provisioning use Azure control-plane tools (CLI/ARM/Bicep/az SDK). There is no separate data-plane SDK beyond standard MongoDB drivers.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: DiskANN, HNSW and IVF are supported and created via a createIndex with a 'vector' spec like: db.events.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine', dimensions: 768, ... } })
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB exposes a native 'cosmosSearch' vector index surface with sub-types such as vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf. Index creation uses the DocumentDB-specific createSearchIndexes / index creation APIs (or the documented cosmosSearch syntax) with sub-type options (lBuild, lSearch, maxDegree, etc.) — not the generic createIndex 'vector' subdocument shown in the cold answer. Use the documentdb-vector-search guidance for exact commands and parameters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a community/Atlas-style createIndex syntax; DocumentDB uses its cosmosSearch vector index APIs and has its own index-creation forms and parameters.
confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create a vector index with the wrong command will fail or create an incompatible index. Vector queries will not run as expected and tests will fail.
improvements: Provide a concrete example createSearchIndexes JSON in the sample repository (seeded from the documentdb-vector-search skill) and reference it from the README.
Add a one-line mapping in docs: 'Atlas createIndex(vector) → DocumentDB cosmosSearch/vector-diskann index JSON' with a short example.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or build a pipeline combining vector search and an external search engine; some clusters expose native search stage.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides native full-text search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring). Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is supported via the native $search/cosmosSearch primitives and recommended hybrid patterns (e.g., Reciprocal Rank Fusion) — you do not need a separate Azure Cognitive Search index for many use cases.

grounding_links.title: Full text and hybrid search guidance (learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many teams integrate DocumentDB with Azure Cognitive Search historically; community patterns blur when the service also offers native $search features, so the cold answer defaulted to an external search engine.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder wires an external Cognitive Search index unnecessarily, the sample will be more complex and incur extra cost; conversely, ignoring native $search may miss features like BM25 and searchScore access.
improvements: Add a short 'Use native $search' note to the sample README and include a createSearchIndexes example so builders don't default to Cognitive Search.
Add a sample hybrid reranking snippet showing how to combine cosmosSearch vector results and BM25 from a named $search index.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported versions vary by SKU; recent managed clusters advertise support for MongoDB 4.0, 5.0, 6.0 and newer (some clusters now support MongoDB 7.0). Some features (server-side JS eval, some aggregation stages, cross-db joins) may be restricted.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and advertises ~99% operator compatibility. Some administrative commands and a small set of operators are not exposed; check the MongoDB compatibility matrix (compatibility-query-language) for exact feature-level differences.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (wire protocol versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none (cold answer was hedged and mostly accurate).

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Cosmos DB emulator for the SQL API (Mongo emulator limited) or use official MongoDB Docker image on port 27017; vector features unavailable locally.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides an official Gateway Docker image for local development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260. Use the Gateway image and follow the documentdb-local-deployment guidance (TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for dev) rather than assuming the Cosmos emulator or vanilla mongo:7.0 for parity with vector / search features.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many developers default to the Cosmos DB emulator or generic mongo docker images; DocumentDB supplies a Gateway image (port 10260) for dev parity including vector/search features.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo:7.0 container or the Cosmos emulator will miss DocumentDB-specific features (cosmosSearch vector/search, exact port/TLS defaults), leading to integration test differences and failing index commands.
improvements: Add a tiny 'Local dev' section to the sample README pointing to the Gateway image and showing a docker-compose snippet that binds 10260 and sets SKIP_INIT_DATA / INIT_DATA_PATH.
Mention the TLS and tlsAllowInvalidCertificates guidance for local dev explicitly in the README.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams depend on the managed cluster providing a replica-set/oplog interface; some services expose them but not universally; enable oplog or ensure replica-set SKU provides it.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams; for multishard clusters a preview feature flag (Change streams for multishard clusters) may have to be enabled in the cluster Features page. Change streams are used for online migrations and are documented with enablement steps.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious — correct that change streams require cluster capabilities; Learn docs add the precise enablement step for multishard clusters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder expects change streams by default on a multishard cluster and doesn't enable the feature, online migration/testing using change streams will fail.
improvements: In the sample README, add a short note: 'If your target cluster is multishard, enable Change streams for multishard clusters under Settings → Features before running migration/stream-based verification.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server for data-plane inspection; the general Azure MCP server does not necessarily include the Mongo/DocumentDB-specific tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides the data-plane tools (aggregation, index management, explain) for Azure DocumentDB. The Azure MCP server is present but the specialized documentdb server is the authoritative data-plane toolset.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft offered a service called DocumentDB which was the precursor to Azure Cosmos DB; the managed MongoDB-compatible offering is surfaced through Cosmos DB (Mongo API) or as a separate managed offering depending on SKU. The open-source 'DocumentDB' project is unrelated — Microsoft’s DocumentDB was a proprietary hosted database product that later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: The naming and lineage are nuanced: the new vCore product was previously marketed as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and has been renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)'. This service is distinct from (a) the original 2014–2017 DocumentDB product that became Cosmos DB and (b) Amazon DocumentDB. The open-source DocumentDB engine (the engine that powers this vCore product) exists and is linked from Microsoft docs. In short: the current service was formerly 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and is now 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore)'; Cosmos DB for NoSQL / RU remains a separate family.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming & history)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple renames and overlapping product names (DocumentDB, Cosmos DB, Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore) plus an open-source 'DocumentDB' engine create historical ambiguity in community and older docs.

confusion_sources.title: Historical Cosmos DB DocumentDB blog posts and older docs

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong product name in docs or code comments may confuse operations teams or cause the wrong CLI/Bicep paths to be followed. It matters for infra and subscription-level guidance.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming history' blurb to any new sample README explaining: (1) this sample targets vCore 'Azure DocumentDB' (formerly 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'), (2) it's separate from RU-based Cosmos DB, and (3) it's not Amazon DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The engine is the managed service's proprietary backend (Azure Cosmos DB engine or the managed MongoDB service) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol via a compatibility layer. That means application code using standard MongoDB drivers generally works, but semantics differ in edge cases.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the project is public). Applications use standard MongoDB drivers and largely do not need code changes, but there are service-specific semantics and a small set of unsupported admin commands/operators — verify compatibility with the published compatibility matrices.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (engine and portability)
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (engine & compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer called the engine 'proprietary' while the current vCore product is explicitly described as built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; the practical consequence (driver compatibility caveats) is correct.
confusions.build_risk: Minor: miscategorizations of engine provenance do not break the sample, but inaccurate wording in docs will confuse maintainers and users about portability and license implications.
improvements: Correct README wording to say: 'Powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine; use standard MongoDB drivers but consult the compatibility matrix for operator-level differences.'

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the event embedding field named 'embedding' with algorithm HNSW, cosine distance and the correct dimensionality. Example: db.journey_events.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_hnsw', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine', dimensions: 768, efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB recommends creating a cosmosSearch vector index (vector-diskann/vector-hnsw/vector-ivf) via the DocumentDB vector index APIs (createSearchIndexes / cosmosSearch index definitions). Pick vector-diskann for production and HNSW for small corpora; include the exact 'dimensions' matching the chosen embedding model. Do not rely on community createIndex(vector) syntax — use the documentdb-vector-search skill's example index JSON.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used Atlas-style createIndex syntax; DocumentDB exposes cosmosSearch/vector-diskann APIs and has different parameter names and a different index-creation path.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong index creation API causes index creation to fail and vector query stages to error. The sample must use DocumentDB-native index forms.
improvements: Add a ready-to-run createSearchIndexes JSON snippet for the sample's chosen embedding dim in the repository (use the documentdb-vector-search skill's vector-create-diskann example).
Document that embedding dimensionality must match the chosen embedding model and show how to change it in the seed script.

confusions.question: What aggregation stage sequence will implement first-touch, last-touch and linear attribution?
confusions.cold_answer: Use $match (window), $sort by timestamp, $group by customerId to push events array and count; then compute first-touch by taking first events[0], last-touch by last item, and linear by unwinding events and distributing 1/numEvents per source.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct approach: $match by window, $sort by timestamp, $group per customer pushing ordered events (or use $first/$last in a single-pass $group when possible), then compute models (first-touch: $first, last-touch: $last, linear: unwind events and assign fractional credit). A compound index on { customerId: 1, timestamp: 1 } is recommended to cover the $match+$sort pattern.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: none

confusions.question: How will the app authenticate to the cluster at runtime in this sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI env var and pass to pymongo.MongoClient(documentdb_uri). The URI contains user/password and TLS options.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the sample should read the connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and pass it to MongoClient. The README/.env.example must show a placeholder only (never store real secrets). When using Entra ID, examples should show the OIDC connection string pattern.

confusions.question: What collection and document layout will the sample create for customer journey events and attribution outputs?
confusions.cold_answer: journey_events: { customerId, timestamp, channel, eventType, value, embedding } and attribution_results: { customerId, version, generatedAt, windowStart, windowEnd, models: { first_touch: {...}, last_touch: {...}, linear: {...} } }
confusions.grounded_answer: These shapes are appropriate: a journey_events collection with per-event docs keyed by customerId+timestamp (index { customerId:1, timestamp:1 }) and an attribution_results collection storing one versioned document per customer with models object for each attribution model. Keep docs <16MB and include schemaVersion/versioning as advised by documentdb-data-modeling.

The sample repo should pick a target Python version and pinned requirements.txt. No skill or doc in the inventory prescribes the sample's exact runtime or pinned dependency versions.

information_gaps.title: Seed data size and exact seed documents
information_gaps.description: The sample run environment says 'load sample data' but does not supply a canonical seed dataset (size, distribution, or fields). The builder must define a small synthetic dataset and include an idempotent seed script; documentdb-local-deployment provides seed guidance but no content.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Deploy or target the vCore product resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).

Use SRV-style cluster URIs (mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/...) with tls=true and retryWrites=false (or explicit authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID) — do not reuse older :10255 / .mongo.cosmos.azure.com examples.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create vector indexes using DocumentDB-native cosmosSearch/vector-*-style index definitions (documentdb-vector-search guidance) and create full-text search indexes with createSearchIndexes and query via $search (documentdb-full-text-search) — do not attempt Atlas or generic createIndex vector syntax.
Use pymongo and the singleton MongoClient pattern; read the connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI and never commit credentials — show a .env.example placeholder instead.
